title: Iran War's One-Two Punch of Oil and Rates Costs U.S. Households $1,700 Each
excerpt: A Moody's Analytics tally puts the total cost of the U.S.-Iran conflict at about $1,760 per American household — $930 of it from energy, $425 from higher interest rates, and $405 from military spending.
body:
• The U.S.-Iran war has cost American households about $1,760 each since fighting began, according to a Moody's Analytics analysis as of September 11 — more than half from higher energy prices.
  • Consumers have spent over $121 billion extra on energy since the conflict started, while the 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level in 19 years, raising borrowing costs for homes and cars.
  • Gasoline has climbed above $4.15 a gallon and diesel hit a record $5.90, and Goldman Sachs warns crude could reach $120 a barrel if attacks on Middle East shipping continue.

A double squeeze on the household budget

American consumers are being hit from two directions at once. Rising oil prices from the U.S. war with Iran are driving up costs at the pump, while a surge in Treasury yields is making everything bought on credit — homes, cars, credit cards — more expensive. The combined bill per household since the conflict began is roughly $1,760, according to an analysis from Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi.

"Consumers are under a lot of financial pressure," Zandi said. The breakdown: $930 — more than half the total — comes from higher energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Another $425 stems from higher interest rates since the war broke out, and the final $405 from higher military spending that Zandi said consumers will ultimately foot through expanded national debt or higher taxes.

Fuel costs alone exceed $100 billion

The energy numbers are stark. Cumulatively, Moody's found that U.S. consumers have spent more than $121 billion extra on energy since the war began. A separate Wall Street Journal analysis put the extra fuel spend at $100 billion, and a cost tracker from Brown University's Watson School of International and Public Affairs estimated Americans have spent $100.9 billion more on gasoline and diesel — about $770 per household — compared with what fuel would have cost without the war.

Prices show why. Gasoline has climbed above $4.15 a gallon nationally, while diesel reached a record $5.90, up from $3.76 before the conflict. Diesel's rise matters beyond the pump: trucks, trains and farm equipment run on it, so higher diesel costs feed into the price of nearly everything shipped. "We're looking at a fall that's going to be the most expensive ever for gasoline, but really for diesel," said Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser at Gulf Oil, warning it would "fuel every aspect of inflation."

Rates rise when relief is needed most

The unusual cruelty of this episode is that borrowing costs are rising at the same time. Normally a geopolitical shock pushes investors into Treasurys, lowering yields and offering households some relief. Not this time: the 10-year Treasury yield jumped this week to its highest in 19 years, and was up 2 basis points Tuesday to 5.040% intraday — its highest since July 19, 2007 — while the 30-year rate hit 5.369%.

The synchronized move reflects investors treating the conflict as an inflation risk rather than a growth risk. "The correlation between yields and oil prices is at its highest level for seven years," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. Brent crude is on track to pass $100 a barrel for the first time since July, and is up more than 60% this year. Goldman Sachs has warned oil could surge to $120 a barrel if attacks on Middle East shipping don't stop.

Escalation, not resolution

The price action follows a sharp escalation. U.S. Central Command said late Tuesday it had attacked five Iranian crude-oil vessels — four in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island, which handles 90% of Iran's oil exports — after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice in two days. Tehran responded by striking a U.S. military base in Jordan, two U.S. Navy vessels and eight oil tankers it said were passing through a "prohibited and unsafe" part of the Strait of Hormuz.

President Donald Trump, asked Wednesday about oil above $100 a barrel, predicted prices would tumble "right after the election," referring to November's midterms. "I think for gasoline, we'll get them below $2 a gallon," he said, adding that the war would "end immediately" after the midterms because Iran's leaders are "desperate to try and affect the election."

The inflation ripple

Wholesale prices already show the strain: the producer-price index rose 0.4% in August, with the 12-month rate at 5.4% — near a three-year high — and core wholesale inflation at 4.7%. With consumer-price data due this week expected to show an oil-driven spike, the Federal Reserve faces pressure to raise rates again — which would add yet another layer to the household bill Zandi has tallied.
